title: Deterministic KV-reclamation contract and e2e verification for concurrent batching
creator: Asha Patel
body:
Summary:
We need a deterministic reclamation contract for KV shards that guarantees prefix-consistent memory reclamation under concurrent continuous batching and GPU memory compaction. The goal is to formalize the lease/fence semantics, implement a lightweight runtime harness that verifies the contract end-to-end, and ship mitigations for pathological concurrent eviction + prefetch interactions that can surface as transient correctness bugs or OOMs in heavy production workloads.

Background & motivation:
Continuous batching improves throughput but increases concurrency over the KV cache: many requests may share prefixes, mutate or reference the same cache entries (KV slices), and interact with asynchronous prefetches and compaction. Existing heuristics (LRU, TTL) work well statistically but leave narrow windows where a race between eviction and in-flight requests can either read stale/zeroed data or cause double-free/overaccounting during GPU memory compaction. We've seen two production incidents where a batched request traversed a reclaimed slab during a concurrent compaction pass; rollback mitigations prevented customer-visible corruption, but the root cause is ambiguous eviction semantics under concurrency.

Goals / Acceptance criteria:
- Define a clear reclamation contract describing allowed behaviours (stronger than eventual safety): reclaimed entries must not be observed by any already-accepted request; prefix-affiliated requests must see a consistent view across multi-shard reads.
- Implement a lease-and-fence protocol that composes with LRU and TTL policies and supports prefix anchoring (i.e., pinning prefixes for short windows during in-flight operations).
- Build an e2e verification harness that: runs deterministic concurrency replays, supports randomized workloads (property-based testing), and exercises GPU compaction/defragmentation code paths.
- Run the harness at scale in CI and for a week in staging; no regressions or sporadic memory-safety events.
- Add telemetry and alerts: transient fence-duration breaches, frequent prefix-pin contensions, and shrink/compact failures.

Design overview (decisions we made so far):
1) Lease tokens with monotonic epoch IDs: every request that might read a KV entry obtains a short lease token (epoch# + token id). Eviction requires observing the global epoch advancement and draining or aborting outstanding leases. This avoids races where compaction reclaims memory while a request still references it.

2) Prefix anchors instead of long-lived global pins: when a continuous-batching worker starts processing a prompt that will likely reference a prefix, it acquires a prefix anchor with a bounded TTL (configurable, default 250ms). Anchors are cheap (refcounts in shard metadata) and are integrated with the eviction policy to temporarily prioritize retention for hot prefixes.

3) Two-phase compaction fence: compaction must first mark candidate slabs as quiesced (no new leases allowed), wait for outstanding leases to drain (or force abort after a safety timeout with diagnostics), then perform reclaimed memory movements. If the drain fails but memory pressure is critical, we fall back to a conservative slow-path: stop admitting new batched requests to reduce contention and trigger a manual GC pass.

4) Policy composition: LRU scoring and TTL remain the primary heuristics for evicting items; the reclamation contract layers a correctness fence above these heuristics. The eviction decision produces a reclamation plan (list of slab ranges + prefix hints) which the fence protocol validates before memory is reclaimed.

Trade-offs discussed:
- Latency vs. safety: stronger fencing increases tail latency under bursts (anchors + leases add overhead). We mitigate this with adaptive TTLs and short leases; the harness measures p99 impact and we allow limited backend throttling as a fallback.
- Memory fragmentation: two-phase compaction with fencing incurs temporary double-memory use. We restrict heavy compaction to off-peak windows and prefer in-place trimming when possible.
- Complexity: introducing a lease/fence layer complicates the runtime. We favor a minimal API surface: AcquireLease(entry_id) -> token, ReleaseLease(token), MarkForReclaim(range) -> fence_handle, ConfirmReclaim(fence_handle).

Implementation plan & milestones:
- Week 1 (done): Spec drafted; initial TLA-style invariants written (see Confluence link). Small spike: implement token mechanism and basic refcounted prefix anchors in the shard metadata (branch: github.com/redwood-inference/serving/PR-evict-lease-spike).
- Week 2 (in progress): Implement two-phase compaction hooks; add fence handles to eviction pipeline; unit tests for fence lifecycle.
- Week 3: Build deterministic replay harness that can: capture request traces, replay them against a single-shard deterministic executor with configurable scheduling, and inject compaction pauses. Add property-based tests (Hypothesis-style) for lease drain conditions.
- Week 4: Run harness across CI matrix (small/medium/large batch sizes + simulated GPU compaction), iterate on timeout heuristics.
- Week 5: Deploy to staging with telemetry, run for 7 days under production-like traffic.

Testing & verification strategy:
- Deterministic replay: capture 10k real request traces from production (sanitized) and replay with systematic schedule variations to surface races.
- Property tests: randomize keyspace, prefix distributions, and batch sizes to validate invariants: (1) no request holds a reference to reclaimed address, (2) prefix-consistent multi-shard reads return consistent versions or fail-fast.
- Stress cluster: run a fleet test that forces rapid alloc/free cycles and triggers compaction; observe memory graphs and fence timeouts.
- Formal model checks: the TLA+ invariants include safety (no use-after-free) and liveness (eventual reclaim under no contention). We run model-checker on a reduced abstraction to catch protocol-level bugs.

Runbook for incidents:
- If fence drain counts increase above threshold -> automatically disable aggressive compaction and increase anchor TTLs for 5 minutes; page on-call if drain count persists.
- If memory fragmentation causes OOM despite fencing -> fallback to admission-control (throttle/buffer) and schedule immediate out-of-band compaction under low-load.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should we permit lease preemption for very old leases (force abort) or always wait for graceful drain? Decision tentatively: time-bound preemption with rich diagnostics.
- How to expose anchor visibility in per-route cost telemetry without leaking customer data? Proposal: expose aggregate counts/latencies.
- Can we extend the fence model to multi-node shared caches? Out of scope for this ticket but noted as future work.

Artifacts & links:
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/KV/Deterministic+Reclamation+Contract (draft)
- Spike branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4121
- Deterministic harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-harness (internal)
- Perf dashboard (staging): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv-reclaim/eviction-fence-staging

Review feedback (so far):
- Lina Chen (Runtime): prefers stronger guarantees for prefix anchoring under cross-shard requests; asked for an explicit multi-shard coordination plan. Action: add coordinator shim to orchestrate fence handles across shards (next PR).
- Jordan Mills (SRE): requested more telemetry around forced aborts and suggested we throttle compaction schedule based on node-level free memory trends. Action: add compaction hysteresis in the scheduler.

Next steps (short):
- Finish compaction hooks and fence lifecycle tests (Marco) — target 2026-03-19.
- Wire harness into CI and run nightly regression (Asha + QA).
- Prepare staging rollout checklist and alert thresholds (SRE + Eng).

Notes for reviewers: please focus on correctness invariants and API ergonomics for the fence tokens. The patch aims to be minimally invasive to the allocator while providing a clear contract for higher-level policies (LRU/TTL/prefix heuristics).
